summary: Records the process and findings of the AAA working group panel that evaluated proposed protocols against the AAA network access requirements in RFC 2989.

eli5.summary: It is a report card on several candidate protocols for checking who you are, what you may do, and what you owe.

questions: which aaa protocol did the ietf panel prefer
subtitle: The report of the panel that scored SNMP, Radius++, Diameter and COPS against the AAA network access requirements.

tldr.problem: The AAA working group needed to decide which candidate protocol could meet its Network Access Requirements for authentication, authorization and accounting.
tldr.mechanism: A panel validated the requirements, had a generous (PRO) and a strict (CON) reviewer score each of four proposals as T, P or F per requirement, then reached a consensus and a summary rating for each.
tldr.outcome: SNMP and Radius++ were not considered acceptable. Diameter and COPS were considered acceptable with engineering, with a slight preference for Diameter.

today: RFC 3127 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the panel's findings as presented in 2000 and builds on RFC 2989.

sections.title: What the Panel Was Asked to Do
sections.content:
This memo records the process and findings of the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) Working Group panel that evaluated proposed protocols against the AAA Network Access Requirements, RFC 2989. The authors say it was rushed to meet the June 2000 Pittsburgh meeting and is not as polished as hoped. It was kept largely as presented so that findings would not appear to change after the fact.

A call for protocol submissions was issued on 4/13/2000. The deadline was June 1, 2000, and submissions needed an unqualified RFC 2026 statement. The panel was announced on May 20, 2000 and chaired by Michael St.Johns, with chairs of related working groups invited. Its mission was to advise the working group and the IESG on the viability of each proposal.
sections.eli5: A team of judges was asked to test four contestants against one checklist and tell the grown-ups which ones are good enough.

sections.title: How the Evaluation Worked
sections.content:
There were three phases: validate the requirements document against the base documents for NASREQ, Mobile IP and ROAMOPS; evaluate each proposal's claims against the validated requirements; and give final recommendations from a side-by-side comparison.

For each of the four proposals, one panelist wrote a PRO brief, which could take the most generous reading and give the benefit of doubt, and another wrote a CON brief using the strictest criteria. Each requirement was scored T (total compliance), P (partial) or F (failed). Where there was a tie, two scores are shown, such as P/T.

Evaluators could use only the source documents or documents they referenced. If something was not written down, it generally did not exist for scoring, so a protocol might meet a requirement but still score lower if the proposal did not show how. Final summary ratings were Not Acceptable, Acceptable Only For Accounting, Acceptable with Engineering (small, medium or large), and Fully Acceptable.
sections.eli5: One judge was kind and one was strict for each contestant. Everyone got T for passed, P for partly, or F for failed, based only on what the contestant had written down.

sections.title: The Four Proposals
sections.content: Four proposals were submitted by the deadline: SNMP (a comparison of SNMPv3 against the requirements), RADIUS enhancements (evaluated as Radius++, with a comparison and an extension framework for RADIUS(v2)), Diameter, and COPS for AAA. All were Work in Progress documents at the time of the report.
sections.eli5: Four contestants entered: an existing management protocol, an upgraded old favorite, a brand-new design and a policy protocol.

sections.title: Requirement-by-Requirement Findings
sections.content:
The consensus scores cover general, authentication, authorization, accounting and Mobile IP requirements. Diameter and COPS scored T on most items. Some notable findings:

  • Fail-over: every protocol scored at best partial, with COPS as T/P. The group thought none did well, and nobody had addressed fail-over in a web of proxies.
  • Proxies and routing brokers: SNMP failed, RADIUS and COPS were partial, and Diameter was the only protocol to address the area to a fair extent.
  • Auditability: SNMP and RADIUS failed, Diameter scored T and COPS P. The panel treated it like non-repudiation and worried digital signatures may be too costly for some equipment.
  • Batch accounting: RADIUS failed, and the panel wondered whether FTP might suit it better.
  • Firewall friendliness: SNMP failed. SNMP and COPS need a firewall to look far into the packet, and Diameter is disadvantaged because SCTP is not well deployed or recognized.

Across the board, the panel found all proposals weak on state reconciliation and on behavior in a web of proxies.
sections.eli5: Most contestants passed the easy questions. They struggled on the hard ones, like what to do if a server goes down or when many middlemen are involved.

sections.title: Verdicts and Recommendation
sections.content:
• SNMP: generally not acceptable as a general AAA protocol. It may have some use for accounting, but the engineering needed for authentication and authorization argues against further consideration.
  • Radius++: not acceptable. It would need substantial engineering, likely ending up close to Diameter's functionality.
  • Diameter: acceptable, needing minor engineering. It might also benefit from a broader data model like COPS.
  • COPS: acceptable, needing minor to medium engineering.

The panel expressed a slight preference for Diameter because its work was further along. It noted that using SCTP as Diameter's transport puts SCTP on the critical path, which could ultimately make COPS faster if SCTP is delayed.
sections.eli5: Two contestants were told they were not good enough. Two could do the job with some fixing, and one had a slight edge because it was further along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that AAA protocols enforce the security of access to the Internet, and that the design of the protocols and of this evaluation took many security requirements as critical issues. A candidate protocol must meet the documented security requirements and be properly engineered and reviewed as it is developed and deployed.

The appendices hold a summary table, comments on the requirements, the PRO and CON briefs, and meeting minutes from teleconferences held in June and July 2000.
sections.eli5: Because these protocols guard the door to the network, the judges treated security as extra important.
